title: "Preoperative Stress Reduction Using Two Cognitive Engagement Interventions During Immediate Preoperative Waiting: A Randomized Controlled Trial"
summary:
Many patients experience anxiety, tension, or stress during the period immediately before surgery. At the same time, opportunities for distraction and the use of familiar coping strategies are often limited in this situation.

The aim of this study is to investigate whether simple engagement activities during preoperative waiting can help reduce stress and anxiety. Two different interventions are compared: a specially developed cognitive activity booklet containing puzzles and mental tasks, and a three-dimensional skill-based puzzle game (Perplexus®). Outcomes will be compared with those of a control group receiving standard preoperative care.

Adult surgical patients with an expected waiting time of at least 15 minutes before the start of anesthesia will be randomly assigned to one of three groups. Stress and anxiety levels will be assessed using brief questionnaires before and after the waiting period. In addition, a short follow-up survey will be conducted on the first postoperative day to evaluate the acceptability, perceived usefulness, and feasibility of the interventions.

The study aims to identify simple, low-cost, and easily implementable approaches that may improve patient support during the immediate preoperative period and can be integrated into routine clinical practice.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Scheduled surgical procedure with an anticipated preoperative waiting time of at least 15 minutes
Presence in the preoperative waiting area (OAE) or anesthesia induction area
Capacity to provide informed consent
Written or otherwise documented informed consent to participate in the study
Exclusion criteria:
Ophthalmologic patients with visual impairment that would preclude meaningful use of the distraction tools
Patients classified as ASA physical status IV or higher
Patients with dementia, relevant cognitive impairment, intellectual disability, or legal guardianship
Refusal to participate or lack of informed consent
Explicit request for pharmacological anxiolysis (e.g., midazolam) before initiation of the intervention; such patients will receive standard clinical care but will not be enrolled in the study
